sections.heading: Finding my deepest joy in knowing you
sections.text: Father, you are the goal my life was made for. My richest joy is not simply to know things about you, but to know you—and to see myself honestly before you. When my mind, desires, emotions, and choices are all turned toward you, I feel most awake. Time with you is never wasted. There is no better use of my hours than honest fellowship with you and a truthful look at my own heart in your presence.
theological_themes: God is the final purpose of human life.
True self-knowledge happens before God, not apart from him.
Communion with God is the believer’s deepest pleasure and highest good.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus describes eternal life in terms of knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent. That grounds the prayer’s claim that knowing God is not a side interest but the heart of real life.
David’s single great desire is to dwell with the Lord and behold his beauty. This supports the longing for communion with God as the believer’s highest delight.

sections.heading: Wanting my whole self to move toward you
sections.text: Draw every part of me into the pursuit of you. I want my thoughts, loves, habits, and longings to stop pulling in different directions and to become united in wanting you. Make me more like you. Teach me to want holiness, not as a performance, but because I want you yourself and the joy of being near you without hiding.
theological_themes: The Christian life involves the whole person being turned toward God.
Holiness is conformity to God and grows out of love for him.
The believer longs not only for God’s gifts but for God himself.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that believers are transformed into the likeness of the Lord as they behold his glory. This directly supports the prayer’s desire for conformity to God through fellowship with him.
The psalm portrays the soul thirsting for God himself and clinging to him. It gives biblical language to the prayer’s longing for full enjoyment of God.

sections.heading: Watching my heart because I love you
sections.text: Give me a careful and tender spirit toward you. Let me be more afraid of grieving you than of losing comfort, praise, convenience, or control. You are not a distant judge to me; you are my blessed God, my Father, and my friend. Because I love you, I want to please you. Guard me from making peace with anything in me that offends you.
theological_themes: Holy watchfulness is part of sincere love for God.
Sin matters because it grieves the God who has loved and adopted us.
The fear of offending God is not servile terror but reverent love.

scripture_references.connection: Paul warns believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit, especially in the context of putting away sinful patterns. This supports the prayer’s concern to avoid offending God out of love.
Because believers have God’s promises, Paul calls them to cleanse themselves and pursue holiness in the fear of God. The verse connects reverence, watchfulness, and practical holiness.

sections.heading: Wanting your glory more than self-centered happiness
sections.text: Lord, teach me to measure joy by whether you are honored and delighted in, not by whether I am comfortable or admired. I do not want to chase a happiness that leaves you out. Make it my highest ambition to glorify you, to enjoy you, and to be glad that you are seen as worthy.
theological_themes: Human joy is rightly ordered when it is rooted in God’s glory.
The Christian’s ambition is to honor God above self-centered satisfaction.
Delighting in God and glorifying God belong together.

scripture_references.connection: Paul gives the broad principle that even ordinary actions should be done for God’s glory. This grounds the prayer’s desire for all joy and ambition to be God-centered.
Paul’s hope is that Christ would be honored in his body whether by life or death, because Christ is his life and gain. This supports the prayer’s preference for God’s honor above personal comfort.

sections.heading: Putting all my life in your hands
sections.text: I want all my time to belong to you—at home, on the road, in work, in rest, in conversations, and in hidden moments no one else sees. I place my worries, plans, responsibilities, and desires into your hands. Make me willing to be fully at your disposal. Free me from the need to run my life as though it were my own private kingdom.
theological_themes: Every place and circumstance can be lived before God.
Surrender means entrusting concerns and plans to God’s wise rule.
The believer belongs to the Lord in life’s ordinary details.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says believers do not live or die to themselves but belong to the Lord. This supports the prayer’s surrender of time, plans, and personal claims to God.
Paul calls Christians to do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus with gratitude to God. That gives biblical shape to offering ordinary life—home, travel, work, and speech—to God.

sections.heading: Making you my only end
sections.text: Help me live to you forever. Be the final reason behind what I choose, what I refuse, what I love, and what I become. Kill the sinful self-love in me that wants your gifts without your rule. Let me not protect, excuse, or feed that old selfish life even in one small corner. Make me yours—gladly, wholly, and without reserve.
theological_themes: God is the believer’s final end and supreme allegiance.
Sanctification includes the putting to death of sinful self-rule.
Christian surrender is whole-life devotion, not partial religious interest.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the Christian life as no longer centered on the self but lived by faith in the Son of God who loved and gave himself for us. This supports the prayer’s desire to live wholly to God rather than to the sinful self.
Jesus calls his disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross daily, and follow him. This grounds the prayer’s strong language about rejecting sinful self-love and yielding entirely to God.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s language about having “no will or interest of my own” could be misunderstood as the erasure of human personality or responsible agency. The adaptation renders it as wholehearted surrender to God’s rule, not the destruction of creaturely identity.

The phrase “never more in one instance love my sinful self” is intentionally severe. It has been kept in substance as rejection of sinful self-love, while avoiding the implication that a Christian should despise personhood or deny God’s good creation.

The original’s reference to the “rational, immortal soul” reflects a traditional Christian anthropology. The adaptation preserves the practical point—honest self-knowledge before God—without pressing philosophical details about the soul beyond the prayer’s devotional intent.
significant_interpretive_choices: “God of my end” and “make thee my last and only end” were interpreted as God being the final purpose and supreme goal of life, not merely the one who controls the end of life or death.

“Rather than be happy in myself” was rendered as rejecting self-centered happiness apart from God, not as rejecting joy itself. The original clearly values joy, but joy rightly ordered around God’s glory and presence.
“Holy watchfulness” and “godly jealousy over myself” were expressed as careful attention to the heart because of love for God, rather than anxious introspection or scrupulosity.
